title: Non-right-angled triangles
summary: The [[sine-rule|sine rule]] and the [[cosine-rule|cosine rule]] find missing sides and angles in any triangle, not just right-angled ones. Area $= \tfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$ gives the area from two sides and the angle between them.

goals.text: Use the sine rule to work out a missing side.
Use the sine rule to work out an angle, including an [[obtuse-angle|obtuse angle]] when two triangles fit.
Use the cosine rule to work out a side or an angle, and choose the right rule.
Use area $= \tfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$, forwards and backwards.

synonyms: area of a triangle half ab sin C
trigonometry in non right angled triangles
find an angle with the cosine rule

before.prompt: Two angles of a triangle are $25^{\circ}$ and $37^{\circ}$. Work out the third angle, in degrees.
before.hint: The angles of a triangle add up to $180^{\circ}$.
before.explain: $180 - 25 - 37 = 118$. It is between $90^{\circ}$ and $180^{\circ}$, so it is obtuse. Revise angle types in {{lesson:4.1}}.

before.prompt: A right-angled triangle has hypotenuse $9$ cm. The side opposite angle $\theta$ is $4$ cm. Work out $\theta$ in degrees, to 1 d.p.
Without a calculator, write down $\sin 30^{\circ}$ as a decimal.
before.hint: It is one of the exact values.

blocks.text: Sine, cosine and tangent from {{lesson:6.2}} need a right angle. The [[sine-rule|sine rule]] works in any triangle.
Label the angles $A$, $B$ and $C$. The side across from angle $A$ is $a$, and so on.

blocks.alt: Triangle ABC with A at bottom left, B at bottom right and C at the top. Side a is BC, across from angle A. Side b is CA, across from angle B. Side c is AB, across from angle C. Each angle and its opposite side are drawn in the same colour.
blocks.caption: Each side is named after the angle across from it.

blocks.text: It is on the formula list. Use it when you know a side and the angle across from it: a matching pair.

blocks.statement: In any triangle, $b\sin A = a\sin B$. Dividing by $\sin A\sin B$ gives the sine rule.
blocks.why: Draw the height $h$ from $C$, at right angles to the line through $A$ and $B$. The two right-angled triangles give $h = b\sin A$ and $h = a\sin B$. If $A$ or $B$ is obtuse, the height lands outside the triangle, and $\sin(180^{\circ} - x) = \sin x$, below, gives the same result.

blocks.text: To find a side, write the side you want over the sine of its angle, equal to the known pair. If that angle is missing, use the angle sum first.

blocks.question: Without a calculator: in triangle $ABC$, angle $A = 30^{\circ}$, angle $C = 105^{\circ}$ and $BC = 12$ cm. Work out $AC$, leaving your answer as a surd.
steps: $BC$ is across from angle $A$: that is the known pair. $AC$ is across from angle $B$.
Check: $B$ is bigger than $A$, so $AC$ should be longer than $BC$. $12\sqrt{2} \approx 17.0$, more than $12$.

blocks.text: To find an angle, flip both fractions so the sines are on top: $\frac{\sin A}{a} = \frac{\sin B}{b}$. On a calculator paper, set degree mode first.

blocks.statement: $\sin(180^{\circ} - x) = \sin x$. For example, $\sin 30^{\circ}$ and $\sin 150^{\circ}$ are both $0.5$.
blocks.why: The sine graph in {{lesson:6.4}} is symmetrical about $90^{\circ}$.

blocks.text: So an [[obtuse-angle|obtuse angle]] can share its sine with an acute one. $\sin^{-1}$ only gives the acute angle, $x$. The angle could also be $180^{\circ} - x$, if that plus the given angle is less than $180^{\circ}$.
When both fit, two triangles match the information: the ambiguous case. The question or diagram tells you which one it wants.

blocks.alt: A horizontal base line starts at A. A side of length 12 goes up from A to B at 35 degrees to the base. From B, a side of length 8 can swing down to meet the base line at two points, C1 nearer A and C2 further away. A dotted arc shows the path of the swinging side through both points. The angle at C1 is obtuse, 120.6 degrees. The angle at C2 is acute, 59.4 degrees.
blocks.caption: With $AB = 12$, $BC = 8$ and $A = 35^{\circ}$, side $BC$ can land in two places.

blocks.question: In triangle $ABC$, $AB = 12$ cm, $BC = 8$ cm and angle $A = 35^{\circ}$. Angle $C$ is obtuse. Work out angle $C$.
steps: Angle $A$ is across from $BC = 8$: the known pair. Angle $C$ is across from $AB = 12$.
$\sin^{-1}(0.86036\ldots) = 59.357\ldots^{\circ}$. This is the acute answer, at $C_2$ in the figure.
The obtuse answer is $180^{\circ} - 59.357\ldots^{\circ} = 120.642\ldots^{\circ}$. Test: $120.6^{\circ} + 35^{\circ} < 180^{\circ}$, so this triangle exists.
Angle $C$ is obtuse, so $C = 120.6^{\circ}$ to 1 d.p.

blocks.text: Quick test: if the side across from the known angle is at least as long as the other given side, the angle you find is acute. Then there is only one triangle.

blocks.prompt: In triangle $XYZ$, angle $X = 52^{\circ}$, angle $Y = 46^{\circ}$ and $YZ = 8.3$ cm. Work out $XZ$ in cm, to 3 s.f.
blocks.hint: $YZ$ is across from angle $X$. Which angle is $XZ$ across from?

blocks.prompt: In triangle $KLM$, $KL = 7.6$ cm, $LM = 10.4$ cm and angle $K = 68^{\circ}$. Work out angle $M$ in degrees, to 1 d.p.
blocks.hint: Angle $K$ is across from $LM$. Put $\sin M$ on top.
blocks.explain: $\sin M = \frac{7.6\sin 68^{\circ}}{10.4} = 0.6775\ldots$, so $M = 42.65\ldots \approx 42.7^{\circ}$. The known angle faces the longer side, so $M$ can't be obtuse.

blocks.prompt: In triangle $PQR$, angle $P = 28^{\circ}$, $QR = 5$ cm and $PQ = 9$ cm. Angle $R$ is obtuse. Work out angle $R$.
blocks.hint: Find the acute answer first. Which obtuse angle has the same sine?
blocks.explain: $\sin R = \frac{9\sin 28^{\circ}}{5}$, so the acute answer is $57.68\ldots^{\circ}$ and $R = 180^{\circ} - 57.68\ldots^{\circ} \approx 122.3^{\circ}$. $15.1^{\circ}$ comes from swapping the $5$ and the $9$.

blocks.text: Pairing a side with an angle at one of its ends. In the sine rule, each side goes with the angle across from it.
With two sides and the angle between them, or all three sides, no side comes with its opposite angle. The sine rule can't start, so use the [[cosine-rule|cosine rule]].
Angle $A$ is between sides $b$ and $c$, and $a$ is across from it. When $A = 90^{\circ}$, $\cos A = 0$ and you get Pythagoras' theorem.
To find an angle, rearrange. Learn this form: it is not on the formula list.
A negative top makes $\cos A$ negative, so $A$ is obtuse. $\cos^{-1}$ gives that obtuse angle directly, so there is no ambiguous case.

blocks.question: Without a calculator: in triangle $PQR$, $PQ = 5$ cm, $PR = 8$ cm and angle $QPR = 60^{\circ}$. Work out $QR$.
steps: The $60^{\circ}$ angle is between the two known sides, and $QR$ is across from it.

blocks.question: A triangular flower bed has sides $4.6$ m, $5.3$ m and $8.4$ m. Work out its largest angle.
steps: The largest angle, $\theta$, is across from the longest side, $8.4$ m, so $8.4^{2}$ is the one you subtract.
$\theta = \cos^{-1}(-0.43703\ldots) = 115.915\ldots^{\circ}$, so $\theta = 115.9^{\circ}$ to 1 d.p. The cosine is negative, so an obtuse angle is right.

blocks.text: Which rule? A side and the angle across from it: sine rule. Two sides and the angle between them, or three sides: cosine rule.

blocks.prompt: A triangle has sides $7$ cm and $10$ cm with an angle of $118^{\circ}$ between them. Work out the third side in cm, to 3 s.f.
blocks.hint: $\cos 118^{\circ}$ is negative, so you subtract a negative number.

blocks.prompt: A triangle has sides $6$ cm, $8$ cm and $12$ cm. Work out the angle $\theta$ across from the $12$ cm side.
blocks.hint: Subtract $12^{2}$ on top, and put $2 \times 6 \times 8$ underneath.
blocks.explain: $\cos\theta = \frac{6^{2} + 8^{2} - 12^{2}}{2 \times 6 \times 8} = \frac{-44}{96}$, so $\theta \approx 117.3^{\circ}$. $62.7^{\circ}$ comes from losing the minus sign, and $156.4^{\circ}$ from forgetting the $2$ underneath.

blocks.text: Working out $b^{2} + c^{2} - 2bc$ and then multiplying by $\cos A$. Work out $2bc\cos A$ as one number, then subtract it.
Area $= \tfrac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}$ needs the height. Often you know two sides and the angle between them instead.

blocks.alt: Triangle ABC with C at bottom left and B at bottom right, so side a is the base CB. A is at the top, and side b joins C to A. A dashed line goes straight down from A to the base, meeting it at a right angle. This is the height h. The angle C is marked between sides a and b.
blocks.caption: The height is $h = b\sin C$.

blocks.text: In the right-angled triangle on the left, $h = b\sin C$. Put that into $\tfrac{1}{2} \times a \times h$.
$C$ must be the angle between sides $a$ and $b$. The formula is on the formula list, and it works for obtuse angles too.

blocks.question: Without a calculator: a triangle has sides $12$ cm and $9$ cm, with an angle of $150^{\circ}$ between them. Work out its area.
steps: The $150^{\circ}$ angle is between the two sides, so use $\tfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$.

blocks.question: A triangle has sides $8.5$ cm and $10$ cm, and its area is $36$ cm$^{2}$. The angle between the two sides is acute. Work out this angle.
steps: $180^{\circ} - 57.9^{\circ} = 122.1^{\circ}$ gives the same area, but the question says acute.

blocks.prompt: Two sides of a triangle are $14$ cm and $17.5$ cm, with an angle of $72^{\circ}$ between them. Work out the area in cm$^{2}$, to 3 s.f.
In triangle $LMN$, $LM = 8$ cm, $MN = 11$ cm, angle $LMN = 52^{\circ}$ and angle $MNL = 46.1^{\circ}$. Work out the area.
blocks.hint: Which angle sits between the sides $LM$ and $MN$?
blocks.explain: The angle between $LM$ and $MN$ is at $M$, so the area is $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 8 \times 11 \times \sin 52^{\circ} \approx 34.7$ cm$^{2}$. $31.7$ uses the $46.1^{\circ}$ angle, and $69.3$ forgets the $\tfrac{1}{2}$.

blocks.text: Using an angle that is not between your two sides. If the included angle isn't given, work it out first.
Sine rule: a side and the angle across from it. Cosine rule: two sides and the angle between them, or three sides.
$\sin(180^{\circ} - x) = \sin x$: if $\sin^{-1}$ gives $x$, the angle could also be $180^{\circ} - x$, if it fits with the other angles.
In a triangle, a negative cosine means an obtuse angle.

mistakes: Leaving the calculator in radians. $\sin 35$ then shows $-0.428$, impossible in a triangle. Check for D or DEG first.
Taking the calculator's acute angle when the angle is obtuse. Work out $180^{\circ}$ minus it, and check the angle sum.
In the cosine rule for an angle, subtracting the wrong side or losing the minus sign. Subtract the square of the side across from the angle.
Rounding a side and then using it again. Keep the full value, or use Ans, and round only at the end.
examTips: For "calculate" or "work out", write the rule with your numbers in, such as $\frac{AC}{\sin 45^{\circ}} = \frac{12}{\sin 30^{\circ}}$. That line earns the method marks.
Give angles to 1 d.p. and lengths and areas to 3 s.f., unless told otherwise. Write a longer value, such as $115.915\ldots$, before you round.
Without a calculator, use exact values such as $\sin 30^{\circ} = \tfrac{1}{2}$ and $\cos 60^{\circ} = \tfrac{1}{2}$, and show them in your working.
When a later part uses an earlier answer, use the unrounded value. A wrong earlier answer used correctly can still earn the later marks.
